title: Mum's tablets
stem:
You are an F2 doctor. On Saturday morning your mother phones. She has run out of her blood pressure tablets (amlodipine, once a day), and her GP surgery is closed until Monday. She feels well.

She asks if you could "just write a prescription" for her, since you are a doctor.
instruction: Rank in order the following actions in response to this situation (1 = Most appropriate; 5 = Least appropriate).

options.text: Write her a month's supply on a hospital prescription.
options.brief: Prescribes for family and misuses hospital resources.
options.detailed: Hospital prescriptions are for hospital patients. Using one for your mother is inappropriate prescribing and a misuse of resources. It is the least appropriate option.

options.text: Suggest she calls NHS 111 for an out-of-hours prescription.
options.brief: An appropriate route, though usually slower.
options.detailed: NHS 111 can arrange for a prescriber to issue a prescription when the surgery is closed. It is appropriate, but often slower than a pharmacy, so it ranks second.

options.text: Advise her to wait until Monday and phone her GP surgery.
options.brief: Probably safe for a short gap, but avoidable.
options.detailed: Missing a day or two of a blood pressure tablet is unlikely to cause harm in someone who feels well, but it isn't necessary when other routes exist. It ranks third.

options.text: Suggest she asks a community pharmacist for an emergency supply.
options.brief: The quickest appropriate route for a regular medicine.
options.detailed: Pharmacists can often supply a regular medicine in an emergency without a new prescription. It is quick, uses her own records, and avoids you prescribing for a family member, so it ranks first.

options.text: Write her a private prescription for a week's supply of the tablets.
options.brief: Prescribing for a close family member should be avoided except in an emergency.
options.detailed: This isn't an emergency, and you don't have her records. Prescribing for those close to you risks a lack of objectivity and poor continuity of care. It ranks fourth because it is at least limited and openly a private prescription.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you avoid prescribing for a family member when appropriate alternatives exist.
explanation.keyDetails: It's a regular medicine. She feels well. Pharmacies and NHS 111 are available. It isn't an emergency.
explanation.reasoning: [D] uses the quickest appropriate route, [B] is appropriate but slower, and [C] is probably safe but unnecessary. [E] prescribes for family without an emergency, and [A] also misuses hospital resources.
explanation.competing: [C] might reasonably rank higher for a drug where a short gap is harmless, but the key prefers getting her tablets today when there's an easy way to do so.

references.title: Good practice in proposing, prescribing, providing and managing medicines and devices
references.note: Prescribing for yourself or those close to you.
